TRADE SECRET EVIDENTIARY PRIVILEGE (EVID. CODE §§ 1060-1062) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Corp.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes California's trade secret evidentiary privilege, set out in Evidence Code sections 1060 through 1062, and the criminal-proceeding procedures that accompany it. It is prepared by Jane Doe concerning a matter involving Acme Corp. and John Smith, identified by case number 24CV012345 in Superior Court of California, County of Santa Clara, and concerning the following trade secret: the proprietary formulation described in the complaint. Section 1060 creates a privilege letting the owner of a trade secret (or the owner's agent or employee) refuse to disclose the secret, and prevent others from disclosing it, in a judicial, administrative, or other proceeding, subject to a fraud/injustice exception. Sections 1061 and 1062 then set out a specific procedure, available in criminal proceedings, for a protective order limiting who may see the secret and for closing part of a criminal proceeding to the public to keep the secret from being disclosed. This document explains what the text of these three sections says and does not say. It is separate from, and does not repeat, the corpus's existing Trade Secret Pre-Discovery Identification Information Sheet (which addresses Code of Civil Procedure section 2019.210 and Civil Code section 3426.5, civil-discovery-sequencing and civil-protective-order provisions of the Uniform Trade Secrets Act), Criminal Trade Secret Theft Information Sheet (which addresses Penal Code section 499c's definition of the criminal offense itself, not courtroom secrecy procedure), Trade Secret Injunctive Relief Standards Information Sheet, and Trade Secret Preemption Doctrine Information Sheet. None of those documents describe the evidentiary privilege or the criminal-proceeding protective-order and closure mechanics covered here. This document does not itself assert the privilege, does not draft or file a motion for a protective order or for closure of a proceeding, and does not evaluate whether any specific information qualifies as a trade secret.

THE TRADE SECRET PRIVILEGE AND ITS FRAUD/INJUSTICE LIMIT
Evidence Code section 1060 gives the owner of a trade secret — or the owner's agent or employee, if either of them claims it — a privilege to refuse to disclose the secret and to prevent another person from disclosing it. The statute's text conditions that privilege on a single stated limit: the privilege applies only if allowing it will not tend to conceal fraud or otherwise work an injustice.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If he or his agent or employee claims the privilege, the owner of a trade secret has a privilege to refuse to disclose the secret, and to prevent another from disclosing it, if the allowance of the privilege will not tend to conceal fraud or otherwise work injustice."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1060 (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1060 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1060.)
  Known gap: Section 1060's text does not itself define "trade secret," does not state in which kinds of proceedings (civil, criminal, or administrative) the privilege may be claimed, and does not describe any procedure for claiming it or for a court to decide whether the fraud/injustice exception applies. The specific motion-and-affidavit procedure described in the companion clauses below, drawn from section 1061, applies only "during a criminal proceeding" by that section's own terms; section 1060's text supplies no comparable procedure for civil or administrative proceedings.

DEFINITIONS BORROWED FOR THE CRIMINAL-PROCEEDING PROCEDURE
For purposes of section 1061 itself, and of sections 1062 and 1063, Evidence Code section 1061(a) defines "trade secret" by cross-reference to the definition in Civil Code section 3426.1(d) (the Uniform Trade Secrets Act's definition) or, alternatively, to the definition in Penal Code section 499c(a)(9) (the criminal trade secret theft statute's definition). Section 1061(a) separately defines "article" by cross-reference to Penal Code section 499c(a)(2).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) For purposes of this section, and Sections 1062 and 1063:(1) “Trade secret” means “trade secret,” as defined in subdivision (d) of Section 3426.1 of the Civil Code, or paragraph (9) of subdivision (a) of Section 499c of the Penal Code."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(a) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1061.)
  Known gap: Section 1061(a) states that these definitions apply "for purposes of this section, and Sections 1062 and 1063"; its text does not say whether the same definitions govern the general privilege stated in section 1060 itself, which contains no definition of "trade secret" of its own. This document did not independently compare the Civil Code 3426.1(d) and Penal Code 499c(a)(9) definitions to determine whether they are identical in scope; section 1061(a) offers them as alternatives ("or") without stating whether they differ.

MOTION, AFFIDAVIT, AND OPPOSITION PROCEDURE FOR A CRIMINAL-CASE PROTECTIVE ORDER
Section 1061(b) sets out a procedure that applies whenever the owner of a trade secret wishes to assert the section 1060 privilege during a criminal proceeding. The owner must file a motion for a protective order (or the prosecution may file it on the owner's behalf and with the owner's permission), supported by an affidavit based on personal knowledge that lists the affiant's qualifications, identifies without revealing the alleged trade secret and the articles disclosing it, and presents evidence that the secret meets the statutory definition; the motion and affidavit must be served on all parties. Any party may oppose the motion by submitting affidavits based on personal knowledge; those opposing affidavits are filed under seal but must be provided to the trade secret owner and to all parties, and neither the owner nor any party may disclose them to anyone other than counsel of record without prior court approval.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The owner of the trade secret shall file a motion for a protective order, or the people may file the motion on the owner’s behalf and with the owner’s permission."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(1) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1061.)
  "The affidavits shall be filed under seal, but shall be provided to the owner of the trade secret and to all parties in the proceeding."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(2) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1061.)
  Known gap: This procedure applies, by its own text, only "during a criminal proceeding"; the statute's text does not extend this specific motion-and-affidavit mechanism to civil or administrative proceedings, and does not state a deadline, measured from any specific event in the criminal proceeding, by which the motion must be filed.

STANDARD FOR GRANTING A PROTECTIVE ORDER AND THE OPTIONAL IN-CAMERA HEARING
Under section 1061(b)(3), the party moving for a protective order must show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that issuing the order is proper; the court may rule without an evidentiary hearing, but may in its discretion hold an in-camera evidentiary hearing limited to the trade secret owner, the prosecution's representative, the defendant, and defense counsel. Section 1061(b)(4) then states the standard for granting the order: if the court finds that a trade secret may otherwise be disclosed during the criminal proceeding and that issuing a protective order would not conceal a fraud or work an injustice, the court shall issue a protective order limiting the use and dissemination of the trade secret and of articles disclosing it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The movant shall, by a preponderance of the evidence, show that the issuance of a protective order is proper."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(3) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1061.)
  "If the court finds that a trade secret may be disclosed during any criminal proceeding unless a protective order is issued and that the issuance of a protective order would not conceal a fraud or work an injustice, the court shall issue a protective order limiting the use and dissemination of the trade secret, including, but not limited to, articles disclosing that secret."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(4) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(4) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1061.)
  Known gap: Section 1061(b)(3)'s text does not define "preponderance of the evidence" or list what evidence suffices to meet it, and it makes the in-camera hearing entirely discretionary with the court ("the court may choose to hold" one) rather than something a movant can compel. The statute's text also does not state what happens if the court neither holds a hearing nor grants the motion outright — for example, whether further briefing may be ordered.

PERMISSIBLE (NOT MANDATORY) CONTENTS OF THE PROTECTIVE ORDER
Section 1061(b)(4) lists provisions a protective order "may, in the court's discretion, include": limiting dissemination of the trade secret to counsel and their staff and to law enforcement or clerical officials; requiring the defendant to view the secret only in the presence of counsel; requiring court approval before showing the secret to anyone not designated by the order, including a vetting procedure for any expert who would receive it; barring public filing of articles disclosing the secret without court approval and notice to the owner; and any other order the court deems necessary to protect the trade secret's integrity.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "That the trade secret may be disseminated only to counsel for the parties, including their associate attorneys, paralegals, and investigators, and to law enforcement officials or clerical officials."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(4)(A) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(4)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1061.)
  "Other orders as the court deems necessary to protect the integrity of the trade secret."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(4)(E) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(4)(E) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1061.)
  Known gap: Every listed provision is introduced with "may" — the statute's text makes each one an option the court can choose to include, not a required term of any protective order, and subsection (E) makes the list expressly non-exhaustive ("other orders as the court deems necessary"). The text does not rank the options, does not say which combination is presumptively appropriate, and does not state a standard for reviewing an expert the court has already approved if new information later emerges.

A PROTECTIVE-ORDER RULING DOES NOT DECIDE TRADE SECRET STATUS OR BIND CIVIL LITIGATION
Section 1061(c) states that a ruling granting or denying a motion for a protective order under subsection (b) is not to be construed as a determination that the alleged trade secret is or is not a trade secret, and that such a ruling has no effect on any civil litigation. Section 1061(d) states that the section has prospective effect only and does not invalidate protective orders entered before it took effect.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Such a ruling shall not have any effect on any civil litigation."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(c) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1061.)
  "This section shall have prospective effect only and shall not operate to invalidate previously entered protective orders."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(d) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1061.)
  Known gap: Section 1061(c)'s text addresses effect on "civil litigation" specifically; it does not state what effect, if any, the ruling has on a different criminal proceeding or on an administrative proceeding involving the same alleged trade secret. Section 1061(d)'s "prospective effect only" language is tied to a 2003 effective date for the version of the statute fetched in this research session; the statute's text does not itself restate what procedure, if any, governed protective-order motions filed before that date.

CLOSING PART OF A CRIMINAL PROCEEDING TO THE PUBLIC TO PROTECT A TRADE SECRET
Evidence Code section 1062(a) lets a court, in a criminal case, exclude the public from part of a criminal proceeding on motion of the trade secret owner (or the prosecution with the owner's consent), if the proponent of closure demonstrates a substantial probability that the trade secret would otherwise be disclosed to the public during that proceeding and a substantial probability that disclosure would cause serious harm to the owner, and if the court finds no overriding public interest in an open proceeding. The same subsection states a limit: no evidence may be excluded under this section if doing so would conceal a fraud, work an injustice, or deprive the prosecution or the defendant of a fair trial.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "in a criminal case, the court, upon motion of the owner of a trade secret, or upon motion by the People with the consent of the owner, may exclude the public from any portion of a criminal proceeding where the proponent of closure has demonstrated a substantial probability that the trade secret would otherwise be disclosed to the public during that proceeding and a substantial probability that the disclosure would cause serious harm to the owner of the secret, and where the court finds that there is no overriding public interest in an open proceeding."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(a) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1062.)
  "No evidence, however, shall be excluded during a criminal proceeding pursuant to this section if it would conceal a fraud, work an injustice, or deprive the People or the defendant of a fair trial."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(a) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1062.)
  Known gap: Section 1062(a)'s closure authority applies, by its own text, "in a criminal case"; the statute's text does not address closing a civil or administrative proceeding to protect a trade secret. The text does not define "substantial probability," "serious harm," or "overriding public interest," leaving those standards' practical content to case law that was not verified in this research session (see the companion clause on this document's case-law limitation).

SCOPE OF CLOSURE, APPELLATE REVIEW, AND LATER PUBLIC ACCESS TO THE TRANSCRIPT
Section 1062(b) requires that any closure motion be preceded by an in-camera hearing limited to the trade secret owner, the prosecution's representative, the defendant, and defense counsel, with a court reporter present, and that the hearing transcript and any articles presented at it be sealed. Section 1062(c) requires the court, before granting closure, to close only the portion of the proceeding necessary to prevent disclosure and to state on the record that the moving party met its burden and that closure will not deprive the prosecution or the defendant of a fair trial. Section 1062(d) allows the trade secret owner, the prosecution, or the defendant to seek relief from a closure ruling by petitioning a higher court for extraordinary relief. Section 1062(e) requires that once a portion of a proceeding is closed under this section, a transcript of the closed proceeding be made available to the public as soon as practicable, with the court redacting any trade-secret information first.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "the court shall close only that portion of the criminal proceeding necessary to prevent disclosure of the trade secret."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(c) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1062.)
  "a transcript of that closed proceeding shall be made available to the public as soon as practicable."
  — Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(e) (Leginfo official text), Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1062.)
  Known gap: Section 1062(e)'s text requires public release of the transcript "as soon as practicable" but sets no specific deadline in days or a comparable fixed measure. Section 1062(d)'s text does not state the standard of review an appellate court applies to a petition for extraordinary relief from a closure ruling, and this document does not address section 1062(f) (concerning witnesses under a related section 1061 protective order remaining in the courtroom during a closed proceeding), which was excluded from this document because the fetched official text of that subsection contains an apparent typographical error ("pursaunt" for "pursuant") that this document did not attempt to interpret or correct.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This Information Sheet was prepared by Jane Doe on January 1, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. It reflects a review of the official text of Evidence Code sections 1060, 1061, and 1062 concerning a matter involving Acme Corp. and John Smith in Superior Court of California, County of Santa Clara, case number 24CV012345, and concerning the following trade secret: the proprietary formulation described in the complaint. Nothing in this Information Sheet is an assertion of privilege, a motion for a protective order, a motion for closure of a proceeding, or a filing in that or any other action.
